title: Preliminary
shortDescription: The opening chapter: the Sanhita's name, when and where it applies, its key definitions, and the general rules for reading it.
summary:
Chapter I is the foundation of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. It does not create offences; instead it sets up how the whole code is named, when and where it applies, what its key words mean, and the general rules for reading it.

Section 1 gives the Act its short title ("Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023"), lets the Central Government bring it into force by notification (allowing different dates for different provisions), and fixes its reach. Every person is liable to punishment under the Sanhita for offences committed within India (territorial application). It also reaches beyond India (extraterritorial application) to offences by any citizen of India anywhere in the world, by any person on a ship or aircraft registered in India wherever it may be, and — newly — to any person anywhere who commits an offence targeting a computer resource located in India. A savings clause leaves laws on mutiny and desertion in the armed forces, and special and local laws, untouched.

Section 2 is effectively a glossary of 39 clauses. It defines the key terms used throughout the code — words like "act," "child," "dishonestly," "fraudulently," "document" (which now expressly includes electronic and digital records), "good faith," "gender," "number," "public servant" and "movable property" — and its last clause says that words not defined here take the meaning given in the Information Technology Act, 2000 or the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Because these definitions apply across every later chapter, they are best studied as a dictionary.

Section 3 sets out the general explanations — the reading rules for the whole code, in nine sub-sections. Every offence is to be read subject to the General Exceptions in Chapter III, even though those exceptions are not repeated in each section. An expression explained in one part means the same everywhere. Property held by a person's spouse, clerk or servant on that person's account counts as in that person's possession, and words referring to acts also cover illegal omissions. The rest of the section governs liability when several people are involved: common intention makes each person liable as if he acted alone; an offence can be committed partly by an act and partly by an omission; whoever intentionally does one of several acts that together make up an offence commits it; and people taking part in the same criminal act can still be guilty of different offences depending on their own state of mind.

Note for exams: the age of criminal responsibility (a child under seven, and a child between seven and twelve of immature understanding) is not in Chapter I. It is in sections 20 and 21, among the General Exceptions in Chapter III.

keyPoints.point: Section 1 — Short title, commencement and application
subPoints: Short title: the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
Comes into force on a date the Central Government notifies (different dates allowed for different provisions)
Territorial: every person is liable for offences committed within India
Extraterritorial: applies to offences by any citizen of India anywhere
Applies to offences by any person on a ship/aircraft registered in India, wherever it is
Applies to any person anywhere targeting a computer resource located in India (new)
Savings clause: does not affect army/navy/air-force mutiny-desertion laws or special/local laws
Fixes the meaning of key terms used throughout the code
'child' = a person below eighteen years of age (clause 3)
'dishonestly' = doing anything intending wrongful gain to one or wrongful loss to another (clause 7)
'document' now expressly includes electronic and digital records (clause 8)
'fraudulently' = doing anything with the intention to defraud, but not otherwise (clause 9)
'gender': the pronoun 'he' applies to male, female or transgender (clause 10)
'good faith' = done with due care and attention, not mere honesty (clause 11)
'number': singular includes plural and plural includes singular (clause 22)
'person' includes a company or association, incorporated or not (clause 26)
Undefined terms take meanings from the IT Act, 2000 or the BNSS, 2023 (clause 39)
(1) Every offence is read subject to the General Exceptions, even though they are not repeated
(2) An expression explained in one part has the same meaning throughout
(3) Property held by a spouse, clerk or servant on your account is in your possession
(4) Words referring to acts also cover illegal omissions
(5) Common intention: each person is liable as if he did the act alone
(6) Joint act needing criminal knowledge/intention: each joiner with it is liable
(7) Causing an effect partly by act, partly by omission is the same offence
(8) Intentionally doing any one of several acts making up an offence = committing it
(9) People in the same criminal act may be guilty of different offences

fastRevision: Chapter I is 'Preliminary' — sets up the code; it does not create offences.
s.1 — short title: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
s.1 — comes into force on a date the Central Government notifies by Official Gazette.
s.1 — different dates may be appointed for different provisions.
s.1 — territorial: every person liable for offences committed within India.
s.1 — extraterritorial: applies to any citizen of India committing an offence anywhere beyond India.
s.1 — applies to any person on a ship or aircraft registered in India, wherever it may be.
s.1 — NEW: applies to anyone anywhere targeting a computer resource located in India.
s.1 — 'offence' (for extraterritorial reach) includes acts abroad that would be punishable if done in India.
s.1 — Illustration: an Indian citizen who commits murder abroad can be tried in India.
s.1 — savings clause: does not affect army/navy/air-force mutiny-desertion laws or special/local laws.
s.2 — Definitions: a 39-clause glossary used across the whole code.
s.2(3) — 'child' means a person below 18 years of age.
s.2(7) — 'dishonestly' = intent to cause wrongful gain to one or wrongful loss to another.
s.2(8) — 'document' includes electronic and digital records.
s.2(9) — 'fraudulently' = doing anything with the intention to defraud, but not otherwise.
s.2(10) — 'gender': 'he' is used of any person — male, female or transgender.
s.2(11) — 'good faith' = done with due care and attention (not mere honesty).
s.2(21) — 'movable property' = all property except land and things attached to the earth.
s.2(22) — 'number': singular includes plural, and plural includes singular.
s.2(26) — 'person' includes a company/association, incorporated or not.
s.2(33) — 'voluntarily' covers effects intended, or known/believed to be likely.
s.2(36)-(37) — 'wrongful gain' = gain of property one is not entitled to; 'wrongful loss' = loss of property one is entitled to.
s.2(29) — 'reason to believe' = sufficient cause to believe a thing.
s.2(39) — undefined terms take meanings from the IT Act, 2000 or the BNSS, 2023.
s.3 — General explanations: nine reading rules applying throughout the code.
s.3(1) — every offence is read subject to the General Exceptions, though not repeated.
s.3(2) — an expression explained anywhere means the same everywhere.
s.3(3) — property held by a spouse, clerk or servant on your account is in your possession.
s.3(4) — 'acts' include illegal omissions.
s.3(5) — common intention: each is liable as if he acted alone.
s.3(7) — an offence can be caused partly by act and partly by omission.
s.3(8) — doing one of several acts that make up an offence = committing it.
s.3(9) — people in the same act can be guilty of different offences.
Age of criminal responsibility is NOT in Chapter I — it is in ss.20-21 (General Exceptions).
Understanding s.2 and s.3 helps you interpret every later offence correctly.

- Territorial: offences within India

- gender, number, person, public servant

- Same meaning throughout

- Acts include illegal omissions
